questions.stem: A 47 year old man wakes with severe pain in his left big toe the morning after running a half-marathon in hot weather. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, shiny and swollen, and he cannot bear the bedsheet touching it. He is otherwise well. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute monoarthritis of the first MTP joint in a dehydrated man is classic gout; pseudogout favours the knee and wrist of older patients.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: cannot bear the bedsheet touching it
running a half-marathon in hot weather
steps.x: Sudden, exquisitely tender **first MTP joint** in a man after **dehydration** = podagra.

elim: Spreading skin infection, not an exquisitely tender single joint woken with overnight.
Gradual, activity-related pain without a red, hot joint.
Favours larger joints such as the knee or wrist in older people.
Possible in any hot joint, but he is systemically well with a near-normal temperature and the classic gout site.

steps.x: **B. Gout.** First MTP + sudden + exquisitely tender = gout. Dehydration and male sex are risk factors.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with acromegaly has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen right wrist. He has never had joint problems before. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 142/88 mmHg. X-ray of the wrist shows linear calcification within the triangular fibrocartilage and no erosions.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray with an acute wrist arthritis points to calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout), associated with acromegaly, hyperparathyroidism and haemochromatosis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: linear calcification within the triangular fibrocartilage
steps.x: Calcified cartilage = **chondrocalcinosis**. A large joint (wrist) plus **acromegaly**, a known metabolic association.

elim: Prefers distal joints such as the first MTP and causes punched-out erosions, not cartilage calcification.
Inflammatory polyarthritis with skin and nail disease; no cartilage calcification.
Symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis with periarticular erosions.
Follows a fall; does not cause a hot joint with calcified cartilage.

steps.x: **B. Pseudogout.** Chondrocalcinosis = pseudogout. Think hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis, acromegaly.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man started treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis 4 weeks ago. He now has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender left first metatarsophalangeal joint. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. His serum urate is raised.
questions.q: Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Pyrazinamide (and ethambutol) raise serum urate and can trigger gout; isoniazid and rifampicin have other classic side effects.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which drug is the most likely cause? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Gout during **anti-TB therapy**: pyrazinamide reduces renal urate excretion.

elim: Causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis, not hyperuricaemia.
Given to prevent isoniazid neuropathy; does not raise urate.
Causes orange secretions, hepatitis and enzyme induction, not gout.
Not part of TB treatment and does not cause gout.

steps.x: **B. Pyrazinamide.** Anti-TB drug + gout = pyrazinamide.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man started chemotherapy for high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma 3 days ago. He now has a hot, swollen, very tender right ankle. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his joint symptoms?
o: Haematogenous spread of bacteria to the joint
Immune complex deposition in the synovium
Urate from rapid tumour cell breakdown
Vitamin D deficiency from reduced intake
questions.e: Cytotoxic treatment of a high-turnover tumour releases purines that are converted to urate, causing hyperuricaemia and acute gout.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his joint symptoms? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: started chemotherapy for high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma 3 days ago
hot, swollen, very tender right ankle
steps.x: Chemotherapy causes **rapid cell death and purine turnover**, so urate rises and crystals precipitate.

elim: Pseudogout is linked to ageing and metabolic disease, not chemotherapy.
Possible on chemotherapy, but the timing after cytotoxic treatment points to a urate load.
Describes reactive or lupus arthritis, not a crystal monoarthritis.
Causes bone pain and weakness, not an acute hot joint.

steps.x: **D. Urate from rapid tumour cell breakdown.** Chemotherapy is a gout risk factor through rapid purine turnover.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has nodal osteoarthritis of her hands, chronic kidney disease stage 3 and takes indapamide. Overnight the distal interphalangeal joint of her left index finger became red, hot and so tender she cannot touch it. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gout favours distal joints and often settles in joints already damaged by osteoarthritis; renal impairment and indapamide reduce urate excretion.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: so tender she cannot touch it
steps.x: Sudden, exquisitely tender **distal** joint plus **CKD** and a **thiazide-like diuretic**.

elim: Spreads across the skin; does not localise to a single exquisitely tender joint.
Usually affects larger joints such as the knee or wrist.
Can affect DIP joints, but is a chronic inflammatory arthritis with skin and nail disease.
Usually a large joint with fever; she is nearly afebrile and has clear gout risk factors.

steps.x: **B. Gout.** Gout = distal, sudden, exquisitely tender. Look for diuretics and CKD.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has firm, painless, yellow-white lumps over both elbows and the backs of several fingers. One over his right elbow has ulcerated and discharges chalky white material. He has had many attacks of painful feet over 20 years. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 146/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Tophi are nodular masses of monosodium urate on extensor surfaces and pinnae in long-standing gout; rheumatoid nodules are not chalky.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: many attacks of painful feet over 20 years
over both elbows and the backs of several fingers
steps.x: Chalky nodules on **extensor surfaces** after years of untreated attacks = **tophi** (monosodium urate masses).

elim: Calcium deposits in systemic sclerosis, with Raynaud's and skin tightening.
Small yellow papules from hypertriglyceridaemia; no chalky discharge or joint attacks.
Bony swellings of the DIP joints in osteoarthritis; they do not discharge.
Firm nodules over the elbows in rheumatoid arthritis, but not chalky and not with attacks of foot pain.

steps.x: **B. Chronic tophaceous gout.** Tophi = chronic tophaceous gout: pinnae and extensor surfaces.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has global developmental delay, writhing involuntary movements and repeatedly bites his lips and fingers. He now has a red, swollen, very painful left big toe. His temperature is 37.2°C and pulse rate 104 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder of purine metabolism causing hyperuricaemia, self-mutilation and gout in children.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Gout in a **child** with **self-mutilation** and dystonia = a disorder of purine metabolism.

elim: Causes motor delay but not self-mutilation with hyperuricaemia and gout.
A chronic arthritis; does not cause self-injury or choreoathetosis.
Affects girls, with hand-wringing and regression.
Seizures, skin lesions and hamartomas; not gout.

steps.x: **C. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.** Child + self-injury + gout = Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint. This is his first ever episode. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. An X-ray of the foot is requested.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the foot?
o: Loss of joint space with osteophytes
Soft tissue swelling with a normal joint space
questions.e: In early gout the joint space is preserved and there is only soft tissue swelling; punched-out erosions appear with recurrent disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the foot? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **first** attack of gout has not yet damaged bone, so the X-ray shows only **soft tissue swelling** and a **preserved joint space**.

elim: Calcified cartilage is the X-ray sign of pseudogout.
Osteoarthritis changes.
Psoriatic arthritis.
Seen only with recurrent, long-standing gout, not a first attack.

steps.x: **E. Soft tissue swelling with a normal joint space.** Early gout X-ray: soft tissue swelling, normal joint space. Erosions come later.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman in a care home has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. She had a similar episode in her left wrist last year that settled. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 132/76 mmHg. The knee has a large effusion.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the knee?
questions.e: Pseudogout characteristically shows chondrocalcinosis, calcified cartilage such as the knee menisci; punched-out erosions belong to chronic gout.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the knee? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Recurrent attacks in the **knee and wrist** of an older woman = calcium pyrophosphate deposition. Its X-ray sign is **chondrocalcinosis**.

elim: Onion-skin periosteal reaction suggests Ewing's sarcoma.
Rheumatoid arthritis.
Chronic gout, which favours the first MTP joint.
Possible, but in an older woman with recurrent large-joint attacks pseudogout typically shows chondrocalcinosis.

steps.x: **A. Calcification of the menisci.** Pseudogout X-ray = chondrocalcinosis (meniscal calcification).

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen left knee. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 140/88 mmHg. The knee is aspirated.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals are monosodium urate, confirming gout even in the knee; rhomboid positively birefringent crystals would mean pseudogout.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The aspirate shows **needle-shaped, negatively birefringent** crystals with a negative Gram stain.

elim: Aspirate would be blood-stained without crystals.
Crystals would be rhomboid and positively birefringent.
Sterile aspirate without crystals, after gut or genital infection.
Gram stain and culture would be positive; the crystals explain the joint.

steps.x: **A. Gout.** Needle + negative birefringence = urate = gout.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man had a hip hemiarthroplasty 3 days ago. He now has a hot, swollen left knee. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. The knee is aspirated: Gram stain shows no organisms and polarised light microscopy shows rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rhomboid positively birefringent crystals are calcium pyrophosphate, confirming pseudogout; gout crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Rhomboid, positively birefringent** = calcium pyrophosphate. Pseudogout often flares after surgery or illness in older people.

elim: Urate crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.
Blood in the joint, not crystals.
Does not produce crystals or a hot knee.
Gram stain is negative and crystals explain the picture; culture should still be awaited.

steps.x: **D. Pseudogout.** Rhomboid + positive = pyrophosphate = pseudogout.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has recurrent kidney stones, constipation and low mood. She now has a hot, swollen right knee. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg. Knee aspirate shows rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Hyperparathyroidism disturbs calcium and pyrophosphate metabolism and is a recognised cause of calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely underlying cause? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: recurrent kidney stones, constipation and low mood
steps.x: Stones, bones, groans and moans with high calcium and PTH = **hyperparathyroidism**, a classic cause of pseudogout.

elim: Also causes pseudogout, but she has no iron overload features and the calcium is high.
Not a recognised cause of hypercalcaemia and stones.
Raises calcium, but with bone pain, anaemia and renal failure, not pseudogout.
Can raise calcium, but the PTH is raised here, pointing to the parathyroid.

steps.x: **D. Primary hyperparathyroidism.** Pseudogout in a younger patient: look for hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis or acromegaly.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has had attacks of pain in his feet for 18 years and never took regular treatment. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 150/92 mmHg. X-ray of his left foot shows well-defined punched-out erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The joint space is preserved.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent gout gives well-defined punched-out erosions with subchondral sclerosis while the joint space is preserved.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: punched-out erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges
steps.x: **Punched-out** erosions with sclerosis and a **preserved joint space** at the first MTP = recurrent gout.

elim: Causes joint space loss and osteophytes, not punched-out erosions.
Shows chondrocalcinosis.
Pencil-in-cup erosions with periostitis, usually with skin disease.
Marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia and joint space loss, usually symmetrical in the hands.

steps.x: **A. Gout.** Punched-out erosions + normal joint space = chronic gout.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man sees his GP with a 3 day history of a red, swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint that is now improving. He has had two similar episodes before. He takes no medication. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg. The GP wants a blood test to support the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: NICE recommends a serum urate level alongside the clinical features to confirm gout; a level of 360 µmol/L or more supports it.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: blood test to support the diagnosis
steps.x: Recurrent podagra in primary care. NICE: use **serum urate** with the clinical picture.

elim: Test for rheumatoid arthritis.
Raised in any inflammation; does not support a specific diagnosis.
Non-specific and used for rheumatoid arthritis.
Relevant to pseudogout associations, not gout.

steps.x: **E. Serum urate.** Blood test for gout = serum urate (NICE).

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen left ankle. He has hypertension and takes bendroflumethiazide. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. The ankle is aspirated and the fluid sent for analysis.
questions.q: Which finding on synovial fluid analysis would confirm gout?
o: Very high white cell count alone
questions.e: Synovial fluid microscopy under polarised light showing needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals confirms gout.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which finding on synovial fluid analysis would confirm gout? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Joint aspiration is the most useful test. Gout = **monosodium urate**: needle-shaped and **negatively** birefringent.

elim: Suggests staphylococcal septic arthritis.
Suggests haemarthrosis.
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals of pseudogout.
Seen in septic and crystal arthritis; does not confirm either.

steps.x: **C. Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals.** Gout crystals: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has had gout for 10 years with four attacks in the past year. He wants to know whether his joints have been damaged before discussing long-term treatment. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to look for joint damage?
questions.e: Plain X-ray shows the punched-out erosions of chronic gout; X-ray changes of destructive joint disease are an indication for urate-lowering therapy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to look for joint damage? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: four attacks in the past year
whether his joints have been damaged
steps.x: Advanced gout: **imaging** shows tophi or **bone erosions**, and X-ray changes are a NICE indication for urate-lowering therapy.

elim: Measures bone density for osteoporosis.
Used for metastases or occult fracture; not to assess gouty erosions.
A bone turnover marker; does not show joint damage.
Can show urate stones but not joint erosions.

steps.x: **C. Plain X-ray of the feet.** Joint damage in gout: start with a plain X-ray.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen left knee. She has never had gout. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg. The knee has a large effusion and she cannot bear weight.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Knee aspiration for microscopy and culture
questions.e: Joint aspiration is the gold standard: rhomboid positively birefringent crystals confirm pseudogout, and Gram stain and culture rule out infection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Any hot swollen joint: **aspirate**. Polarised light microscopy finds crystals and culture excludes septic arthritis.

elim: Shows bone but cannot identify crystals or organisms.
Shows effusion and soft tissue, not the cause.
May show an association, but does not diagnose the joint.
Supports gout but cannot confirm pseudogout or exclude infection.

steps.x: **B. Knee aspiration for microscopy and culture.** Hot joint = aspirate first.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has pseudogout of his right knee confirmed on aspiration. He also has erectile dysfunction, type 2 diabetes diagnosed last year and a liver edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the underlying cause?
questions.e: Haemochromatosis causes pseudogout through disturbed pyrophosphate metabolism; raised ferritin and transferrin saturation are the first tests.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the underlying cause? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Young man with pseudogout, **diabetes**, **hepatomegaly** and hypogonadism = **haemochromatosis**.

elim: Rheumatoid arthritis; does not explain diabetes and hepatomegaly.
Spondyloarthritis association, not pseudogout.
For acromegaly, which would show coarse features and large hands.
For gout; the crystals already show pseudogout.

steps.x: **B. Ferritin and transferrin saturation.** Pseudogout + diabetes + big liver = check iron studies.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has a firm, white, painless nodule on the rim of his left ear and attacks of painful feet for many years. A sample of chalky material from the nodule is examined under polarised light. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 148/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on microscopy?
questions.e: Tophi are masses of monosodium urate, which are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent under polarised light.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on microscopy? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: attacks of painful feet for many years
steps.x: Ear nodule with chalky contents in long-standing gout = **tophus**, made of monosodium urate.

elim: Flat, plate-like crystals seen in chronic effusions; not tophi.
Sarcoidosis.
Calcium pyrophosphate; pseudogout does not form ear tophi.
A squamous cell carcinoma or keratin cyst.

steps.x: **B. Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals.** Tophus contents = urate = needle, negative.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint. He has no other medical problems, normal kidney function and takes no medication. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: NSAIDs such as naproxen are first-line for acute gout when there is no contraindication; urate-lowering drugs are not started during the attack.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no other medical problems, normal kidney function
steps.x: Acute gout in a fit man: first-line is an **NSAID** (or colchicine).

elim: Urate-lowering therapy is not started during an acute attack.
Second-line urate-lowering therapy; not for an acute attack.
Treats infection; this is classic gout.
Used when NSAIDs and colchicine are unsuitable; he has no contraindication.

steps.x: **D. Naproxen.** Acute gout, fit patient = NSAID (naproxen) or colchicine.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has an acute attack of gout in her left knee confirmed by aspiration. She has heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Her kidney function is normal and she has no history of G6PD deficiency. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 132/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Colchicine is the alternative first-line drug when NSAIDs are contraindicated, for example in heart failure; warn about diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
steps.x: **NSAIDs** are contraindicated with a heart failure history, so use **colchicine**, which is safe with no G6PD deficiency.

elim: Not used to treat an acute attack.
NSAIDs worsen fluid retention and are avoided in heart failure.
Urate-lowering therapy, not an acute treatment.
An NSAID, avoided with heart failure.

steps.x: **B. Colchicine.** NSAID contraindicated (CKD 3, ulcer, heart failure, warfarin) = colchicine.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has an acute attack of gout in his right ankle. He has G6PD deficiency and chronic kidney disease stage 3. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 144/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: When both NSAIDs and colchicine are unsuitable, corticosteroids such as oral prednisolone treat acute gout.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**CKD 3** rules out NSAIDs and **G6PD deficiency** makes colchicine risky, so use a **corticosteroid**.

elim: Not started during an acute attack.
Used with caution in G6PD deficiency because of haemolysis.
NSAIDs are contraindicated in CKD stage 3.
Inadequate for acute gout.

steps.x: **D. Oral prednisolone.** Neither NSAID nor colchicine suitable = steroid.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman on haemodialysis for end-stage kidney disease has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint. Her eGFR is 6 ml/min/1.73m². Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Low-dose corticosteroids are used for acute gout in dialysis patients or with eGFR below 10 ml/min/1.73m², where NSAIDs and colchicine are unsafe.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
On **dialysis** or eGFR below 10, the option is **low-dose steroids**.

elim: Not used to treat an acute attack.
Accumulates in severe renal failure and causes toxicity.
Urate-lowering therapy, not an acute treatment.
NSAIDs are contraindicated in advanced kidney disease.

steps.x: **D. Low-dose oral prednisolone.** Dialysis + acute gout = low-dose steroid.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman has pseudogout of her right knee confirmed by aspiration, with a negative Gram stain. She has no history of peptic ulcer, kidney disease or heart failure. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Naproxen with a proton pump inhibitor
questions.e: Acute pseudogout is treated first with an NSAID such as naproxen with PPI cover; allopurinol has no role because urate is not the problem.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no history of peptic ulcer, kidney disease or heart failure
steps.x: Pseudogout ladder: **NSAID + PPI** first, then colchicine, then intra-articular steroid.

elim: Lowers urate; has no role in calcium pyrophosphate disease.
Second step if NSAIDs fail or are unsuitable.
Gram stain is negative and crystals explain the knee.
Reserved for refractory disease after NSAIDs and colchicine.

steps.x: **E. Naproxen with a proton pump inhibitor.** Pseudogout first-line = NSAID with PPI.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man has pseudogout of his left knee. He has taken naproxen with omeprazole and then colchicine for 10 days, but the knee remains hot and swollen. Repeat aspiration shows calcium pyrophosphate crystals and the culture is negative. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Intra-articular corticosteroid such as methylprednisolone is the next step for pseudogout not settling on NSAIDs and colchicine, once sepsis is excluded.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: naproxen with omeprazole and then colchicine
steps.x: Refractory pseudogout after NSAID and colchicine, with infection excluded: **intra-articular corticosteroid**.

elim: Lowers urate; does not treat calcium pyrophosphate disease.
Used for septic arthritis; culture is negative.
Urate-lowering; no role in pseudogout.
No evidence of infection.

steps.x: **D. Intra-articular methylprednisolone.** Pseudogout ladder ends with an intra-articular steroid.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man started allopurinol for recurrent gout 3 weeks ago. He now has a widespread itchy red maculopapular rash. There are no blisters and his mouth and eyes are not affected. He takes colchicine as cover. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue allopurinol and add an antihistamine
Stop allopurinol and later switch to febuxostat
questions.e: Allopurinol rash means intolerance: stop it, because it can progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and use febuxostat as second-line urate-lowering therapy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: started allopurinol for recurrent gout 3 weeks ago
steps.x: **Rash** is a common allopurinol side effect that can progress to **Stevens-Johnson syndrome**. Second-line is **febuxostat**.

elim: Allopurinol rash can progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome, so it must be stopped.
Worsens the reaction.
He still needs urate-lowering therapy for recurrent gout.
Colchicine is not the cause of the rash.

steps.x: **D. Stop allopurinol and later switch to febuxostat.** Allopurinol intolerance = febuxostat.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man had his first attack of gout 4 weeks ago, which settled on naproxen. He has chronic kidney disease stage 3 with an eGFR of 48 ml/min/1.73m². He asks about preventing further attacks. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Allopurinol at a low dose, titrated up
Febuxostat at a low dose, titrated up
No treatment until a third attack
questions.e: Allopurinol is first-line urate-lowering therapy, offered after a first attack and started low and titrated; CKD 3 to 5 is a NICE indication.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate long-term management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: first attack of gout 4 weeks ago

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with chronic kidney disease stage 4 has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint. She takes no diuretics. Her eGFR is 24 ml/min/1.73m² and her serum urate is 560 µmol/L. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hyperuricaemia?
o: Increased purine release from cell death
questions.e: Hyperuricaemia comes from overproduction or underexcretion of urate; in chronic kidney disease, reduced renal excretion is the cause.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hyperuricaemia? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Urate is cleared by the kidneys. **Impaired renal function** means **underexcretion**.

elim: Diet adds little compared with the effect of failing kidneys.
Seen with chemotherapy or tumour lysis.
Not the mechanism in kidney disease.
Relates to pseudogout, not urate.

steps.x: **E. Reduced renal excretion of urate.** CKD causes gout by underexcretion of urate.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy has hyperuricaemia, severe dystonia and bites his fingers until they bleed. His maternal uncle had the same condition. His parents and older sister are well. His temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 108 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the mode of inheritance?
questions.e: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder of purine metabolism; carrier mothers pass it to sons, causing hyperuricaemia and gout.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the mode of inheritance? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: bites his fingers until they bleed
steps.x: Self-mutilation, dystonia and hyperuricaemia = **Lesch-Nyhan syndrome**. Affected males through carrier mothers.

elim: A parent would usually be affected.
Would affect boys and girls equally; the maternal uncle pattern points to the X chromosome.
Passed from mother to all children, both sexes affected.
Affected males pass it to all daughters, and females would also show disease.

steps.x: **E. X-linked recessive.** Lesch-Nyhan = X-linked recessive.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has a 12 hour history of a hot, swollen left first metatarsophalangeal joint. Aspiration shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals inside neutrophils. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the acute inflammation?
questions.e: Monosodium urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, which releases IL-1β and drives the acute neutrophil response of gout.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of the acute inflammation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals inside neutrophils
steps.x: Urate crystals precipitate in synovial fluid and are taken up by cells, activating the **NLRP3 inflammasome** and releasing **IL-1β**.

elim: Mechanism of rheumatoid arthritis.
Septic arthritis; no organisms here.
Lupus or reactive arthritis.
Osteoarthritis; not an acute hot joint.

steps.x: **E. NLRP3 inflammasome activation releasing IL-1β.** Gout inflammation = NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1β.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with recurrent gout had a rash on allopurinol and is switched to febuxostat. His serum urate is 520 µmol/L. He asks how the new tablet works. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of febuxostat?
questions.e: Febuxostat and allopurinol both inhibit xanthine oxidase, reducing conversion of xanthine to uric acid and lowering serum urate.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the mechanism of action of febuxostat? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Febuxostat, like allopurinol, blocks **xanthine oxidase**, so less xanthine becomes uric acid.

NSAIDs.
Colchicine.
Uricosurics such as probenecid.

steps.x: **E. Inhibits xanthine oxidase.** Allopurinol and febuxostat = xanthine oxidase inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with gout and chronic kidney disease stage 3 is treated with colchicine for an acute attack of his right knee. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg. His student doctor asks which cell's activity the drug mainly reduces.
questions.q: Which cell's function is most reduced by colchicine?
questions.e: Colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerisation, reducing neutrophil migration and phagocytosis of urate crystals and dampening inflammation.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man was started on allopurinol by his GP 3 days after a gout attack settled, without any anti-inflammatory cover. Ten days later he has a new hot, swollen left ankle. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this new attack?
o: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition caused by allopurinol
Increased urate production caused by allopurinol
Mobilisation of urate from tissue stores
Reduced renal urate excretion caused by allopurinol
questions.e: Starting urate-lowering therapy too soon after an attack mobilises urate stores and triggers flares, so it is delayed about 2 weeks with 3 months of NSAID or colchicine cover.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of this new attack? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: 3 days after a gout attack settled, without any anti-inflammatory cover
steps.x: Starting **too soon** and **without cover**: the falling serum urate **mobilises urate stores** and triggers a flare.

elim: Gives a rash, not a hot joint.
Allopurinol does not cause pseudogout.
Allopurinol reduces urate production.
Allopurinol does not impair excretion.

steps.x: **D. Mobilisation of urate from tissue stores.** Start allopurinol 2 weeks after the attack, with 3 months of cover.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman has recurrent attacks of a hot, swollen right knee. She has no metabolic disease. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 138/78 mmHg. Aspiration shows rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals and X-ray shows chondrocalcinosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her condition?
o: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition in cartilage
questions.e: Pseudogout results from calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition in cartilage, associated with ageing and with metabolic conditions disturbing calcium and pyrophosphate.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Pseudogout = **CPPD deposition in cartilage**, linked to **ageing** even without metabolic disease.

elim: Septic arthritis; crystals and recurrent attacks point elsewhere.
Calcific tendinitis, mainly of the shoulder.

Rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **B. Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition in cartilage.** Pseudogout = CPPD in cartilage; ageing is the commonest association.
